newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russia delays vote on German trophy art.
newsitem.headline: Russia delays vote on German trophy art.

text.p: Russia's upper house of parliament on Wednesday delayed a vote on the fate of art seized from Nazi Germany in World War Two, sparing President Boris Yeltsin embarrassment during an official visit to Germany.
But the president already faces resentment at home for a vague promise to give Germany some art during his trip, which ends on Friday morning.

"They annihilated 26 millions Russian citizens and we have to pay them, it appears. They are scoundrels, fascists and bastards," flamboyant ultranationalist leader Vladimir Zhirinovsky told a news conference on Wednesday.

In an interview published on Tuesday, Yeltsin, asked by the German magazine Stern if he would bring some of the art treasures in his luggage to Germany, said: "Not the Troy gold, of course. But I'll bring some other items with me."

The gold, unearthed by German archaeologist Heinrich Schliemann in 1873, is part of booty seized by Soviet troops from German museums and homes. Schliemann recorded his find as the property of King Priam of ancient Troy featured in Homer's epic "The Iliad". Bonn wants the treasures back.

Russia's upper house of parliament had been expected to vote on Wednesday on a measure asserting Russian ownership of the art, which also include a priceless Gutenberg bible and paintings by French impressionists Claude Monet and Henri Matisse.

But deputies in the Federation Council, who had been lobbied by the president not to vote during his Germany trip, delayed their decision. They opted instead to ask all deputies to participate in a written ballot, which means a final result could be delayed until the next session in May.
"All deputies...including those absent from the hall, should be responsible for this law," said Mikhail Mashkovtsev, a deputy from the the remote Kamchatka region, who proposed the delay.
The lower house of parliament has already passed the law, overruling a veto from Yeltsin, who went to Germany on Wednesday.
Yeltsin would have to sign the measure into law if the upper house approved it as well, although the Kremlin has said the president would appeal to the constitutional court.

The art has become a pressing issue half a century after World War Two because Russia admitted holding far more trophy art than it previously acknowleged. The Soviet government had hidden it in museum basements and other secret vaults.
Many Russians view the art as compensation for the wartime suffering of the Soviet people and for the many Russian treasures destroyed in the German invasion.
The return of the treasures was expected to on the agenda of the Russian president's talks with Chancellor Helmut Kohl.

During the parliamentary debate on Wednesday, Yeltsin's representative Anatoly Sliva said adopting the law would prevent Russia from recovering 461,588 pieces of art taken from the Soviet Union during World War Two.
But communist deputy Vassily Starodubtsev highlighted the strong resistance to giving back any Germany art.

"The psychological subtext of this law is above all what is important for Russia," he said. "It will be very difficult for Russia to explain that it received no compensation for the destruction, the killing and for the wounded."
